extracted.intended_audience: general readers and policymakers interested in British imperial/military policy and frontier affairs (late 19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative/historical analysis of frontier policy and military practice in British India, assessing systems (short service, forward policy), soldiers' qualities, and administrative/military remedies. Includes appended official despatches illustrating criteria for commendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short service system — quantity versus quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The short service system 'provides enormous numbers' but produces troops of 'poor quality' — youth, want of training and lack of regimental associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The continental system's 'gigantic scale' suits mass armies; Britain adopting short service gained some numbers but 'decreased our standard a good deal.' Evaluate systems by their trade-off between rapid manufacture of soldiers and the resulting individual quality and cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of recruitment method with service system
rubrics_metrics.description: Short service and conscription are inseparable; Britain’s voluntary system makes conscription politically and practically unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the army is recruited by a voluntary system, conscription (necessary for true short-service mass armies) is impractical: 'Without conscription we cannot have great numbers.' Any system assessment must consider the nation's recruitment model and political will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of soldiers for colonial warfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Soldiers sent beyond the seas need to fight hand to hand in hot, pestilential climates against athletic native troops; thus older, experienced, acclimatised men are preferable to boys of twenty-one or twenty-two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate troop fitness by age, prior service, exposure to fire, medals, and acclimatisation: 'Boys of twenty-one and twenty-two are expected to compete on equal terms with Sikhs and Gurkhas of thirty... It is an unfair test.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding assumptions of racial superiority — intrinsic merit as legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominance in colonies rests on 'intrinsic merit' alone; if that is lost, claims to rule fail—not because of moral decline but because our soldiers may be insufficiently developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and military claims should not rest on presumed racial superiority; instead maintain superiority through demonstrable merit (training, discipline, effectiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: What produces soldierly courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage among soldiers is common and explained as largely a simulation achieved by three principal influences: preparation (discipline/training), vanity (reputation among comrades), and sentiment (regimental pride, attachment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To foster courage, emphasise preparation (habit, training, familiarity with danger), cultivate healthy esprit de corps and reputation, and nurture sentimental attachments (regimental identity, traditions, songs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of regimental identity (including naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regimental sentiment contributes to performance; monosyllabic appellations have advantages and foster equal starting points (contrast with overly elaborate territorial titles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage strong, simple regimental identities to strengthen pride and cohesion; avoid cumbersome, fanciful titles that undermine common standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic evaluation of frontier policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Frontier policy must be appraised across military, economic, political and moral facts; the subject is vast and resists facile phrases or epigrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overgeneralisation; take 'broad views' cautiously and balance diverse, specialized knowledge when judging any forward or defensive frontier policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward Policy objective criterion — securing passes and extending influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Forward Policy' aims to obtain the frontier (Gilgit, Chitral, Jelalabad, Kandahar) by extending and consolidating influence over mountain passes—a policy that, when applied to 'barbarous peoples,' implies ultimate annexation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess such policy by clarity of stated aims (control of strategic passes) and recognition of the political consequences (annexation, change in local governance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable consequences of forward occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance brings increased territory and a nearer frontier line but also war: isolated forts are 'challenges' provoking relieving and punitive expeditions, and tribal hostility may be inflamed by perceived threats to independence and priestly authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh territorial gains against the inevitability of resistance, rising costs, and the moral/political fallout among local populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fort construction and garrison adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Forts have sometimes been 'badly constructed—cramped... commanded... without flank defences... without proper garrisons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frontier posts should be well-designed with appropriate defenses (including flanks) and adequately sized garrisons; poor construction and under-garrisoning convert positions into liabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource sufficiency as decisive constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal objection to immediate large-scale military occupation is lack of 'troops nor the money to carry it out.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any proposed military solution must be judged against available manpower and fiscal capacity; absence of resources invalidates certain strategic options regardless of their desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative strategy — gradual political approach required
rubrics_metrics.description: Where full military occupation is unaffordable, the alternative is 'a system of gradual advance, of political intrigue among the tribes, of subsidies and small expeditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pursuing a slow political approach, ensure it is 'consistently pursued' and complemented by reforms (wider powers for political officers, occasional troop demonstrations) rather than weak half-measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subsidies and economic instruments over military force
rubrics_metrics.description: From general survey: 'silver makes a better weapon than steel.' Subsidies can enlist tribal interests on the side of law and order; increasing their wealth lessens barbarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise economic inducements and targeted subsidies to secure cooperation; economic engagement can be cheaper and more effective than prolonged military action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arms-supply policy — government market intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: In the supply of arms, 'the Government would find it cheaper to enter the market as a purchaser, and have agents to outbid the tribesmen, rather than to employ soldiers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use market mechanisms and governmental purchasing power to control arms proliferation among border tribes instead of relying primarily on military suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative candour and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers 'shrink from the legitimate conclusions' and tie their hands by 'ridiculous and unnecessary proclamations'—timidity leads to folly (e.g., desertion of forts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments should frankly lay the case before the public, avoid timid, self-contradictory proclamations, and maintain consistent policies; weak execution of a strong policy is more dangerous than honest admission of constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of inconsistent weak implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong policy weakly carried out is like 'Dynamite in the hands of a child'—dangerous; recognition of facts must be followed by admission and decisive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure follow-through and adequate empowerment of field officers; half-measures and hedging undermine strategic objectives and provoke instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for judging irreversible policy decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Having 'crossed the Rubicon' (advanced beyond the old frontier), the forward movement may be 'beyond recall' and thus requires acceptance that reversal is unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate long-term commitment and acceptability of irreversible actions before initiating them; recognize when policies commit the state to sustained engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic cost-benefit of frontier occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade of frontier valleys 'will never pay a shilling in the pound on the military expenditure necessary to preserve order.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on anticipated local trade to offset military costs; economic viability must be assessed realistically when planning frontier expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for military commendation (from official despatches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers and men are recommended for favorable consideration based on prompt action, reinforcement of outposts, leadership after casualties, gallantry in driving the enemy, dash in leading men, skill and dash in reconnaissance, improving defences, prompt mobilisation and good march discipline, courage when wounded, medical bravery in saving lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete acts under fire (initiative, command ability, bravery, saving comrades, effective reconnaissance, logistical/medical performance) as grounds for recommendation and promotion; despatches enumerate many specific exemplars.
